Mr. Chairman, I have been reading clause 1 and have been following the very well thought out arguments of my colleague, the hon. member for Timiskaming. In my limited understanding of this matter it does seem that we are being asked in effect to buy a pig in a poke. For the benefit of those who may not have followed the refinements of my argument earlier, I was not objecting to the procedures of the house but rather to the fact that there is not a general public law in existence which would permit this group to be incorporated in another way and not by way of statute law.
Private Bills
In the last clause which was read by the hon. member for Timiskaming there is something in its construction which concerns me a bit. It says:
-for the purpose of administering the property, business and other temporal affairs of the Corporation.
These are the objectives and they are spelled out in more detail in subsequent clauses of the bill but particularly they are for the purpose of administering the property, business and other temporal affairs of the corporation. It would seem to me that the word "other" should not be in here because the implication is that the corporation would administer the temporal property, the temporal business and other temporal affairs. It would seem to me we should take out the word "other" to make it clear that we are not interpreting the administering of the property and the administering of the business of the corporation as being temporal affairs, although perhaps in the strict sense of the word it is correct.
When the hon. member for Timiskaming read that I came to the conclusion that the word "other" really was adding a bit of confusion to what the particular propositions of the corporation are. I should like to have some comment from the sponsor of the bill in respect of what the petitioners felt about that aspect, whether they felt anything or whether grammatically it is the correct way to phrase it.
There is another matter which I should like to raise, but in doing so I think I have to make reference to the fact that there is no public law in existence under which such a group can be incorporated. If there were we would have the guide lines or criteria established with regard to what the corporation could or could not do. As it is now parliament has to decide in every individual case what the corporation can or cannot do. Parliament has to decide what is or is not in the public good.
I suggest to the hon. member for Timiskaming that one of the reasons there were not very many questions asked in the committee is that there was not that much interest in the committee and that the members who attended the meeting were not too interested in this particular bill one way or another. I submit that that is an attitude a great number of members take in respect of private bills of this nature. They give lip service to the concept that we have a bounden duty to

March 15, 1966
Private Bills
pass on these matters and that is the extent of their participation.
Parliament is in the position of having to decide whether or not the incorporation of this group, the Evangelistic Tabernacle, will serve the public good and I submit we are not competent to do that. Surely we are being helped in our ignorance of the matter here because clause 1, after it mentions certain individuals, reads:
-together with such other persons-
That is satisfactory.
-and congregations as become members of the religious body-
They do not say what is the religious body to which such other persons and congregations can adhere or join and what constitutes the congregation is extremely vague. In the committee proceedings this matter was mentioned briefly by Mr. Smith asking:
Is there only one congregation of this organization?
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
Mr. Belfoi replied by saying:
The present incorporate corps are a Winnipeg congregation of about 120. There are four other groups, one in Saskatoon, one in Vancouver, one in Okanagan Valley and one in Kenora, Ontario.
Mr. Smith then asked:
Do the other groups have such an incorporation?
To which Mr. Belfoi replied:
No, the other groups do not, but they will all form part of this incorporation, after it is incorporated, of course.
There is no doubt in Mr. Belfoi's mind that the other groups will automatically become an integral part of the incorporated structure which we are now being asked to pass on in this house. If we are always going to be faced with the prospect of determining whether or not in the case of any bill, and with particular reference to the one before us, incorporation of the group will serve the public good, then we shall have to ask the committee to examine all groups and in this particular instance all the other potential congregations, especially the ones mentioned in the reply which I read just a few moments ago. The minute we get into the ludicrous situation of having to examine sundry unknown people and congregations, we might as well ask the Prime Minister to set up another royal commission of inquiry, because the matter will be that extensive.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I respectfully commend this motion to the house. The subject matter, I believe, does not raise differences in a party sense, although I recognize that there may be difference of opinion among members in their individual capacities. It is within the recollection of the house that I made a reasonably lengthy opening statement regarding penitentiaries on the calling of the estimates of the Department of Justice. I therefore do not propose to trench upon the time and patience of the house except to offer two short points in support of the motion.
We are now well into the first half of the ten-year penitentiary plan and I humbly suggest that it would be profitable to examine our physical plant before launching into the second part of the program. I do not conceal from myself or the house that there has been some criticism of our new institutions. The principal target has been the special correctional units, one of which will be completed later this year at St. Vincent de Paul. The penitentiary service appreciates that such criticism is inspired by a genuine interest in this important matter. The building of three other units has been stayed, and I believe it would be worth while for the members of a committee to have a first hand inspection of this one unit so that they would have an opportunity to voice their opinions before we march forward.
A question was raised during the estimates debate whether a penitentiary committee was necessary having regard to the fact that there is a Justice and Legal Affairs Committee already in existence. It is interesting to note that of the 14 members who last year offered enlightened opinions on this important subject of penitentiaries, all of whom I believe are still members of the house, only two are members of the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee. In other words, I am saying that

many members whose training and experience is outside the legal world have a deep and abiding interest in penitentiary affairs and the failure to establish this committee might mean that the house would be deprived of the benefit of their judgment.
I do not, of course, suggest that the members of my own profession are not competent to deal with this matter, but I do want to emphasize that the subject of penal reform in this modern age is no longer the private preserve of judges, jailers and lawyers. The penitentiary service is faced with a building program of formidable dimensions and great urgency. In closing, Mr. Speaker, I renew my plea that this motion be adopted, fpr I believe that a committee can render valuable assistance in drafting the blueprint necessary for the development of our penal institutions in the difficult days ahead.

I am afraid there will be a tendency to look purely at the physical state and condition of the penitentiaries rather than looking at the after effects of incarceration. For years we have had the cycle of arrest, conviction, incarceration and release. Upon release the person has been in the position of starting the cycle all over again. History has proven that it does not really matter what the state of the penal institution is because people still manage somehow or other to get into it. As so-called civilized people we deplore the state of some of our prisons. We think that sanitary facilities are not what they should be. We concern ourselves about the paint, the calcimine, the white-wash, whether the bars are shining, whether the clothes are suitable, whether the food is good, whether the shoes are satisfactory, but we do not concern ourselves with what happens to the individual once he walks out through the gates. The whole emphasis of any study of our penitentiary system must be on this point, to ensure that we are doing as much as we possibly can to see that the human being we lock up in a cell is treated as a human being. The state of the cell really does not matter, although our sensitivities may be offended, because we should concern ourselves with assuring that everything possible is done to give the man the best possible chance of not returning.
This is the point with which the committee should concern itself. This should be the mental orientation of every member of that committee regardless of the fact that it is set up merely to consider the physical facilities that exist. As I said when we discussed this question last year, I think we are approaching the problem from the wrong direction. I emphatically disagree with my good friend the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson), with whom I so often agree when issues are discussed in this house, when he expresses the view, the view of many people in Canada and of many members of parliament, namely that because people have committed crimes, have been brought to trial and been found guilty, the answer is to lock them up.
We have not done much to find better ways of dealing with offenders. Locking a person up does not do much for that person, nor help him in the future. When a person is sentenced to a penitentiary in Canada, he is really being sent to a university of crime.
Some time ago when the son of one of my constituents was sent to a provincial jail for stealing a car, she said to me, "When my son first went to jail he only knew how to start one type of car without a key. When he came out of jail, he could start any car without a key". That is the value of what happened to that boy in jail, and that is the sort of thing that happens to most people whom we send to our penitentiaries. They come out, and then go back a second and third time.

It is proposed that the government spend somewhere in the neighbourhood of $200 million in the next ten years, to build new penitentiaries.
Anybody who has any kind of heart at all will agree that even if people do commit crimes, they should not always be put into penitentiaries. They should not be put into the kind of buildings we have here, the kind of buildings of which St. Vincent de Paul is an example. By building better buildings we shall have accomplished nothing in solving the kinds of problems which make people commit crimes. I know that this is not the place to discuss jails, but we are talking about the spending of $200 million to build buildings. I think it would be better if the minister would come forward and say, "We know on the basis of experience that probation works. Probation keeps 85 to 90 per cent of the people who are handled by the probation service in the province from committing a second crime, and from going to prison possibly a second time."
Surely the minister and the department, instead of talking about spending a tremendous amount of money on buildings to house people who have committed a first, second or third crime, might do better by saying to this house: "We are going to propose to the provinces an expenditure of several millions of dollars which, if they are prepared to match that, would mean that they could expend very large sums on probation services." Certainly probation is the responsibility of the provinces at this time. If the suggestion I put to the house were carried 
out, it would keep people out of the penitentiaries, and that is what I would like to see.
Another thing we are going to propose, Mr. Speaker, is that people with better than grade 10 or grade 11 education be employed at penitentiaries. These people will not just be guards. I am not being critical when I say this, nor am I being critical of people working in our penitentiaries. We have the kind of peoople there we want, and that we are prepared to pay for.
I hope the minister in the very near future, if he cannot do so tonight, will say, "We are going to raise the standards required for a person to get a job in our penitentiaries, and we are going to increase the salary range to get the kinds of people who will not just be guards, but who will be able to do rehabilitation work. We are going to allocate enough money so that we will not just have a few part time psychiatrists."
I happen to know the psychiatrist who works at St. Vincent de Paul. I know his reputation in the field of correction. I am not being critical of him, but a psychiatrist for three half days a week cannot possibly do the job he is supposed to do.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, instead of spending money on buildings, we should be coming forward with a program to take on psychiatrists, psychologists, and teachers who are aggressive and dynamic, who would make prisoners enthusiastic to learn so that they could upgrade their education. It would not be right or proper for us to rest on that report without attempting to go forward.
I commend the minister and the government for continuing the program initiated by the former minister, my hon. friend from Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) to provide for the enlarging of institutions and the construction of new ones across the country. No one who has been in Dorchester penitentiary as often as I have, for short periods of time, can fail to appreciate the difficulty faced by those associated with the Canadian penitentiary service when endeavouring to put rehabilitation programs into effect. It is next to impossible to try to operate such programs when there are far too many individuals incarcerated in our institutions, as a result of which security becomes the thing uppermost in everyone's mind.
I should like to say this to the minister: I believe that at the present time the morale of the staff is anything but good. This has nothing to do with their pay. I realize that everyone wants more money, no matter what job he may be doing. People are always endeavouring to secure new fringe benefits. I appreciate, also, that the government has a new system of pay for its employees under consideration at the present time. It is not this aspect which concerns me. It is the fact that they are uncertain about what is likely to happen with regard to individuals such as Reginald Colpitts, Leopold Dion and Georges Marcotte. They do not know how many more such individuals they are likely to have in a system which was not built to maintain people of this kind.
The guards at Dorchester penitentiary asked for danger pay of $1,000 a year. I do not think they were really concerned whether $1,000 was paid to them. I believe they were more concerned about the government taking action to protect them against inmates of this type. As far as I am concerned, our laws are not geared to allow such inmates to remain in our penitentiary system at the present time. The sooner we get on with the debate on capital punishment, whether for the abolition or retention of the death penalty, the earlier will every man in the penitentiary service be in a better position to know what lies before him. I think this house will be in a better position to know what needs to be done with

this type of individual presently in our institutions. Not until then will we be capable of making the kind of decisions about them that we should be making.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
I would like to say also-and it was inherent in the speech by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow)-that there is a great danger we are getting too soft about those people who go into our institutions. I believe in rehabilitation; I believe in doing everything possible to prepare a man to go back to life in our world, in society, but I believe he should go back only after he has realized he has committed an offence against society, and that to do it again will be to his detriment only.
I do not believe in providing radio facilities, all the other forms of entertainment, and all the other things which are available to a free man in society, to an inmate who has committed dastardly crimes to society, before he recognizes the seriousness of what he has done and is willing and ready to mend his ways and prepare himself for re-entry into society.
I believe, if we are to be practical, we must have maximum, medium and minimum security institutions. I do not believe we have enough to look after not only the population that is in our institutions today but also the population which is entering our institutions every day, and which is continuing and growing at a frightening rate. Certainly there are approaches we have to take which are different, which are new. These approaches are not necessarily to be accepted by everyone, but they are approaches which are far reaching and which in many cases have been proven to be acceptable, to a degree, in other countries of the world.
I believe the parole system we have established today is good. I believe naturally there are holes in it, like there are in anything else, but I do not believe there is anything significantly wrong with the approach we take today toward parole. I do not think there is anything more I would like to say. I would like to repeat however that I do believe this committee will be of value not only to the members who serve on it, but also to parliament. I hope the committee will be set up, set up quickly, and that we will get on with the consideration of this matter.

If I may be permitted to say so, the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) made a short but interesting contribution. I turn now to the remarks of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) who entered a disclaimer of being an expert on penitentiaries. I must do the same thing and say, with some regret, that some of my former clients have much more knowledge of penitentiaries than I possess, but it will be my duty to rectify that situation. The hon. member made the point that penitentiaries are something more than just bricks and mortar, but are essentially people. In reply to him, and the hon. member for Skeena, as I interpret the terms of reference, they will include not only the physical plant, the cells and so on, but also matters such as staff training and such things as the program within the institution to prepare the inmates for their release.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) suggested I made a disastrous statement, and I take his remarks in the spirit in which he made them, because I know he has a genuine interest in this matter. However, I am sure he did not wish to do me any injustice. He was referring to my statement when I said that the inmate population would increase to over 10,000-and he was quite right in the figure he gave. I was only pointing out that with the growth in population and the present trend it would reach this figure. He made a statement concerning probation officers and his remarks fell on sympathetic ears. Over the last year we added 21 new parole officers. I realize it is not a large figure in terms of our inmate population, but it is a step in the right direction.
The hon. member said I should do something about upgrading the staff. We are doing something about it. We are building new staff training colleges in Kingston and in Montreal, and are upgrading the skill and capability of the correctional staff. He also made the interesting statement that perhaps we should not
Consumer Credit Committee be concerning ourselves, nor should the committee concern itself with the matter of putting up new buildings; that we do not need a committee to tell us that we need new buildings. That is not the purpose of the committee. It is to determine the matter of putting up the right type of new buildings. I suggest this is very important.
I thank the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) for his kind remarks and for the support he has given this committee. He said we lag behind in penal reform. I must say I think there is some truth in this, but I think we now are moving forward. There has been developing a new sense of responsibility in this field. The initial impetus for this new sense of responsibility came from the previous administration, and I have no desire to conceal that fact. I hope we can continue it.
I am not suggesting we are going to build a new heaven on earth in our penitentiary service, but I do think we are taking a step forward, and with the co-operation of the committee I think we can make a useful contribution in that direction. I wish to thank all hon. members for their contributions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF SUBSCRIPTIONS BY CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the main objective of the resolution under consideration, namely a measure to amend the Bretton Woods Agreements Act, is to enable Canada to keep on supporting actively the work of the International Monetary Fund by providing for an increased Canadian contribution to the resources of that institution.
The bill provides for the increase of our contribution to the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
Finally, the act will amend the existing act so that the reports submitted to parliament under that act will bear on the calendar year rather than the financial year.
In 1964, at the annual meeting of the international monetary fund, there was considerable support for an increase in the assets of the fund, and its governors, including the Minister of Finance of the day, supported a resolution instructing the board of governors to the fund to see whether it would not be possible to increase their assets by increasing quotas.
At the beginning of last year, the managing director proposed, in his report, a general increase of 25 per cent of all quotas in force on February 26, 1965, subject to deferred payments in the case of less developed countries facing payment difficulties.
The report also recommended additional increases in quotas for 16 member countries, including Canada, in view of the relatively high rate of growth of the economy and foreign trade of these countries, since the last revision of the quotas, in 1959.
Undoubtedly, it is proper for Canada to participate in the general increase in the assets at the disposal of the fund and, in
DEBATES	2741
Bretton Woods Agreements Act addition, to accept a special increase in its quota.
Consequently, the former minister of finance, Mr. Gordon, in his capacity as governor of the fund for Canada, voted in favour of the proposed increase in quotas and the government is now asking the house to approve an amendment to the Bretton Woods Agreements Act, to enable Canada to increase its subscription. Canada has taken an active and leading part in the International Monetary Fund since its establishment in 1946 under the Bretton Woods Agreements Acts.
As a central organization dealing with international monetary problems, the Fund has achieved a noteworthy success in the pursuit of its commendable aims.
The latter, stipulated in the statutes of the Fund, are designed to encourage international monetary co-operation, to promote the development of international exchanges, to promote the stability of exchange, to contribute to the establishment of a multilateral system of international payments with regard to current transactions by making available to its members medium term resources, so as to enable them to make up their deficiencies in the balance of payments without resorting to measures likely to affect international prosperity and to shorten the duration and decrease the intensity of the imbalance of international payments of member states.
The significant success achieved since 1946 in the attainment of these aims has enabled our country to grow and to prosper even though it depends to a great extent on trade and international movements of capital.
If we actively support the Fund, it is because we believe the aims pursued initially are still of current interest and their achievement is very important for Canada.

Certainly there have been charges in the financial pages of the press from time to time by representatives of certain countries that the United States operates directly through its predominant position in the I.M.F. so as to further its own foreign policy. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it always is interesting to note that a measure which very well may affect the lives of everyone in the western world is one that usually excites very little interest either here, in the press, or on the part of the public. I suppose it is because it appears to be a rather dull subject. The measure before us is a fairly simple one, to increase Canada's contribution to the International Monetary Fund and to the World Bank.
There is of course a background to this, Mr. Chairman, which has not yet been made public so far as I know, but which I think can be discussed with a certain discretion. I think it is fairly common knowledge among those who watch these events that there has been a growing concern in recent years about the question of the international liquidity that has been brought about largely by the situation in which the United States finds itself.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
It is three years ago now that I raised this question at an international conference in Belgrade. I pointed out at that time that the rest of the world, a short period before that, had really received notice from the U.S.A. that it was now no longer going to be able to finance, to the degree it had been doing, the exchange reserves of a large part of the world, contributions that were brought about inadvertently, or at least without deliberate purpose, by the development of deficits within the United States. At that time the announcement of the Interest Equalization Act was the notice to which I have referred.
Ever since that time there have been continuing reports in the press of discussions, particularly among the Big Ten countries, of which Canada is one, on the necessity of reconsidering our whole problem of international exchange. I think it is no secret that the Canadian government has been playing a prominent part in these recent conversations and is preparing, if it has not already done so, to present to the other members of the so-called Big Ten, certain proposals for the development of what I would term the new unit of international exchange-a cautious step, shall I say, perhaps in keeping with our usual caution in world affairs, by which we do not quite cut the umbilical cord of gold but we do attenuate it to some extent.
I am reminded that at the time the Bretton Woods Agreements was drafted, the late John Maynard Keynes proposed at that time a new
March 15, 1966	COMMONS
international unit, which he suggested should be called bancor. It is possible that Maynard Keynes made a rather rash comment in introducing his idea at the Bretton Woods conference, pointing out that if the conference accepted his idea it would be the first step toward global administration, which immediately caused a scurry of anxiety and apprehension, and his proposal got no further. I suspect, sir, that before long we are going to have to deal with this in somewhat the same manner that Lord Keynes suggested at Bretton Woods.
We have had a series of currency crises, and there seems no reason that there will not be more currency crises in future, with the great increase in world trade and the growing stringency in international liquidity.
There is another aspect of our problem, Mr. Chairman, which ties in very directly with the question of the International Monetary Fund and its position in the world in the future. That is the relationship between the developed countries and the undeveloped parts of the world where there is, of course, a common saying that the gap between the poor and the rich countries is growing wider and is, to some extent, to be accounted for by the difficulties that the emerging countries have in obtaining sufficient foreign exchange to finance their development.
I would hope that we shall hear more of the proposals of the Canadian government with regard to the new unit of international exchange during discussion of this bill, if it is to be referred to the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, which I hope it will be. And I hope, if it is referred to that committee, that the Minister of Finance will undertake to have appear before the committee some of the leading figures, most of whom are quite readily available in the United States, who have been advancing various ideas for the solution, or at least the amelioration of this problem of international liquidity.
I think, sir, one might say that we are now facing in the international scene somewhat the same situation that national economies faced some 30 years ago when most of the countries were attempting to maintain the gold standard, and were strangling themselves in that attempt. I think we have now reached somewhat the same position internationally; that we are going to have to break away from a fixed relationship that must restrict the expansion of world trade in future unless some
DEBATES	2745
Bretton Woods Agreements Act rough equivalent to the managed currencies with which modern societies operate is found in the international field.
I notice the suggestion of the hon. member for Edmonton West that there might be danger of American domination of the world through the operations of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. It is, of course, quite true that it was at the instigation of the United States that the World Bank withdrew its proposed financing of the Aswan dam in the United Arab Republic, to my mind a disastrous move for which we have been paying ever since.
This may well be the case, but I do not know how you can overcome that because the United States is at the present time the most powerful and wealthy nation in the world. One can only hope that those who are in charge of the United States policy will take a larger view than merely the immediate interests of the United States, and realize that the well-being and prosperity of the American nation is as dependent as that of any other nation on general world prosperity and development, and will be prepared to use their tremendous power and influence towards developing the undeveloped areas of the world and, by that means, ensuring some peace and stability.
I would just conclude by again asking the parliamentary secretary, and through him the Minister of Finance, to consider the referral of this bill to the Committee on Finance Trade and Economic Affairs, and to make arrangements for various people, of whom I am quite sure the Minister of Finance is well aware, to attend and give us some advice as to the possibilities and the dangers that lie before us in the field of international exchange.

Mr. Chairman, in following the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands I would just say we trust that this legislation can be referred to the Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs without much delay. I believe the situation relating to foreign exchange is rapidly reaching a crisis, and something different from what has been done already will be necessary. We in this house will want answers to many of the questions that are in our minds at the present time with respect to the whole area of international settlement. In fact, I would say that the whole area of international settlement, apart perhaps from the international situation in southeast Asia, is the most critical problem
March 15. 1966

Bretton Woods Agreements Act we face on the general scene today. Certainly it is a problem for us here in Canada.
The other day in the financial section of the Globe and Mail, dated March 9, I noticed that our own situation is emphasized by the fact that Canadian borrowings on the United States capital market are running at a rate 11 times more than they were in 1965.
It stated:
A total of $172,880,000 in U.S.-pay Issues had been offered by the end of February by Canadian governments and corporations, compared with only $15,000,000 in the first two months of last year, according to the monthly compilation by Wood, Gundy and Co. Ltd.
Likewise, Mr. Chairman, this point is emphasized on the international front by the fact that the big ten in international finance recently had an important meeting in Europe and, owing to the policies of France, they found themselves in a situation for which it was most difficult to find a solution.
From the limited amount of news which has come from that meeting we find there were three main ideas being presented as alternatives. One of them, and I think it is the one secretary Fowler of the United States treasury is advancing, is that we must retain the present gold standard, with probably a few innovations such as we are being asked to make here, by increasing our own contributions to the International Monetary Fund.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Then there are those who believe that the gold standard must be scrapped altogether and an entirely new basis of exchange provided. There are others who feel that the gold standard must be maintained although it must be modified. Amongst the latter are those who believe that, gold having maintained a constant value for the past 30 years, it must be decreased in value; that it is not reasonable to expect that the standard price of gold 30 years ago should apply or function effectively today; that the cost of living has more than doubled across the world and therefore they advocate a major revision of the gold policy.
The Social Credit party-I say this for the benefit of the hon. member for Edmonton West who made some remarks in this regard a short while ago-advocates a measure that will get us out of the situation we are in, and we believe this can only be done by a completely new approach to the problem of international settlements. We go along with the hon. member who preceded me in saying that in the same way that the gold standard

was put aside in the mid-1930's on a national basis, so the time has come when the gold standard has to be revised at the international level as well. Not until this has been done will we avoid crises such as we have at the present time, in which we are being asked to increase our contribution to help solve this problem of international liquidity.
It is a very serious problem that we face in this regard. It is interesting to note that prior to the time the Bretton Woods Agreements was first reached, Prime Minister Churchill had made a commitment to President Roosevelt that he would do everything he could to get Britain back on to the gold standard in order to strengthen the position of the United States. The situation which they then anticipated, developed following the end of the war. As a result we have now reached the point where there is no question at all that this whole policy of international settlements is tied part and parcel with the policy of the United States treasury. I think it goes even farther than that. I believe it goes right to the whole closed shop for monetary reform that is at the present time operated by the international bankers of the world.
I should like to put on the record a few sentences from "The New Republic" of September 25, 1965, in relation to this problem. The only reason I do so is that it might provide a little background when this bill is considered by the committee and might allow an understanding of the critical situation represented by what this bill proposes to do relating to the over-all picture of international settlements. This article is entitled "Closed Shop for Monetary Reform" and was written by one Nathaniel McKitterick, whose name I think is familiar to most of us. The article reads as follows:
The Benevolent and Protective Order of Central Bankers, gathered this week in Washington-
This was last fall at the last meeting of the International Monetary Fund.
-for the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund, is wrestling with a major constitutional crisis. The Bankers Union has been running the international monetary system for as long as there has been an organized system. They have been running it according to a set of rigid rules which have only been basically and deliberately changed twice and then only in conjunction with two catastrophes-the Great Depression and World War II. Now the bankers face the challenge
of changing the rules in advance of catastrophe_
a challenge they have never met before.
The Bankers Union is in a bind because its jurisdiction over money-or more precisely over
the maintenance of confidence in money_________is
threatened. And good members of the Bankers Union, like good trade unionists, regard their first
March 15. 1966

duty to be protection of their jurisdiction against intrusion by outsiders.
The threat to the bankers' jurisdiction comes, not from another union, but from responsible political leaders-that is, politicians responsible to the voters for their offices. This threat has grown ever since the old gold standard was abolished and responsible political leaders, instead of submitting to the tyranny of gold, started to follow deliberate and discretionary policies to reconcile the often competing objectives of domestic price stability and high employment levels. Now the Bankers Union fears, and with good cause, that responsible leaders may want to reduce the role of gold as an international medium of control in favour of discretionary policies, implemented through the international monetary system, to sustain increasing flows of goods and capital among countries.
The reason why so many people, even some in the Bankers Union, are saying that the rules of the monetary system must be changed is that the present system threatens to force a serious contraction in world trade and investment (and in domestic growth rates in countries particularly short of reserves)-
This is the situation that is developing in the United States today, because their continuing imbalance of trade and foreign credits is something which they realize cannot continue. The article goes on:
-when it ought to be sustaining and encouraging expansion. The present system relies on dollars and pounds sterling to overcome the inability of gold to provide the "liquidity"-the means of payment-to finance expanding world trade and investment.
We may criticize the President of the Republic of France for some of the things he is suggesting in regard to this particular problem, but when one understands the problem that France faces-and it is the problem that many other nations face; it is the problem that Canada faces also-perhaps some of the things he is saying make more sense than we give them credit for. The article continues:
Gold has long since ceased to supply more than a fraction of the needed international reserves; over the past seven years foreign holdings of dollars have accounted for about three-quarters of the total. However, the system has an inherent weakness; the very U.S. payments deficits which make the creation of new reserves possible were deemed by the Bankers Union to undermine foreign confidence in the dollar; central bankers, under the existing rules, could not continue to accumulate dollars in their reserves and in fact began to reduce their holdings by buying U.S. gold.
I might add, in the same way as France has been doing, to a point of danger as far as the system is concerned. The article goes on:
With the elimination of the major source of new reserves-dollars-it is generally agreed that the present system will be unable to generate adequate amounts of "liquidity" in the future.
This is why at the present time it is necessary for the International Monetary
Bretton Woods Agreements Act Fund to come to Canada and ask for an increase in our contribution. The article continues:
In fact, many highly qualified observers, including Sir Roy Harrod, feel that the world is already in need of greatly increased reserves. But even if some of them grant the need privately, it is nearly impossible for members of the Bankers Union to do anything about it in public. Any step to increase reserves, by creating a new international monetary unit to provide the base for expanding world credit, will inevitably grant responsible political leaders a larger discretionary role in the operation of the monetary system than is now the case; any practical reform will change the existing rules somewhat and at least potentially weaken the bankers' jurisdiction as the upholders of confidence in money. It is nearly impossible, constitutionally, for the Bankers Union to address itself to fundamental changes in its rules. Change means risk and risk is something that bankers must avoid if they wish other people to entrust their money to them. The bankers are the prisoners of their occupation, indentured to gold.
I think it would be very revealing to find out just what proposals Canada made at the meeting of the 10 major financial powers, held in Belgium last week. I believe this points up the fact that Canada must take the lead, for her own survival if for no other reason, in bringing forward an alternative proposal in this whole area of international settlements. It means a medium of exchange other than gold, because we in the Social Credit party maintain that gold is just as inadequate today on the international scene as it was in 1935 in Canada.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
So, Mr. Chairman, we are not dealing just with our share of the increased contribution, we are dealing with something that is far more important. It goes back to the basis of the Bretton Woods Agreements itself. It goes back to the problem that developed first during the depression days of the thirties. It became acute during world war II, when we were forced to make changes because of this emergency. During the depression years, world trade had dropped to less than 50 per cent of what it had been during the twenties. When consumer goods came back on the market, trade again became vital to the economy of our nation. The nations were able to bridge the gap for a while longer. However, we are moving into an area where this crisis is just ahead of us. This time, we are faced with the task of having to provide a solution before the crisis reaches us because if it does come upon us it will create a situation even more intolerable than we can visualize if war came again.
March 15, 1966

Bretton Woods Agreements Act
I am convinced, Mr. Chairman, that the only basis upon which the total development of our resources in the world, both human and material, can go forward, is the continued expansion of world trade. It must be possible for us to exchange our goods back and forth as the needs and the markets provide the opportunity. Unless the whole set-up for international settlements is brought in line with this need, then we are going to continue with a situation in which the rich nations get richer and the poor nations get poorer. We have this intolerable situation where millions of people are starving to death in the face of plenty, where we cannot provide for three billion people when there could be twenty billion people within the same area. We are not solving this problem, simply because the closed shop of the bankers' union is more interested in perpetuating the power they now hold than in meeting the greatest need of this world today, namely, an increase in world trade. We need a situation in which the goods that are available, whether they be primary or secondary in nature, are able to reach the people who need them.
After all, the only reason we produce anything is so that we can consume it. The only basis upon which we can interchange these things, be they goods or services, is by the monetary system. The monetary system, as it relates to the particular issue before us, is an international one. I am convinced there will have to be a completely new organization for international settlements, with a new medium of exchange if we are ever going to accomplish the expansion of world trade.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to speak longer. However, I should like to say for the record that I believe this is one of the most inportant problems that we face in this parliament. It is not going to be good enough to go along and say, sure, Canada is a good fellow; Canada is always willing to do her share; Canada is going to put up another $45 million-to perpetuate what? We are doing this to perpetuate the arrangements for international settlements, and those arrangements are not working. They cannot work, because the basis is wrong.
It is not until we realize this fact that we will come up with the suggestions that ought to be made to conferences such as the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund. 1 hope we step out and say that we who can be the bread basket of the world, are willing to set a basis for world trade which the world must have in future years if we are ever

going to have a peaceful development, if we are ever going to meet the needs of human beings.
In closing, I would just say we believe this matter must go to the committee. We hope that when it does the government will agree that we can discuss the matter in greater depth, and we will not be limited to the question of whether or not we intend to make this contribution. I agree we are going to have to make the contribution until some other arrangement is adopted. I emphasize that this is one of the most important problems that faces us so far as the international scene is concerned. This is one area in which we can give leadership, and we can show the United States that the system they are advocating, as Mr. Fowler has said repeatedly during the last few days, is wrong so far as the development of commerce in the world is concerned.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I did not intend to say anything about this world monetary situation, since I came in late. However, I have been a world trader for the last 50 years. Before the first great war we had a unit of settlement in the world and that was the pound sterling. All settlements were made in London, no matter where in the world you were trading. They were made on the basis of the pound sterling. After the first great war, England lost her commerce. She was drained of her gold, and she could no longer act as a world banker.
Before the first great war, England was a free trader. She had a surplus of currency beyond her world requirements and she invested that surplus around the world. She lost money on her investments, but she kept world trade moving. After the first world war, the United States was not a free trade nation. She was a tariff country and she said, we will take your gold but we will not take your products. The United States accumulated a lot of gold.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I attribute the collapse in 1929 to the fact that the United States was not a free trade nation, would not take products but would take gold. When she got all the gold, trade was at a standstill. In my opinion, it is world trade that keeps things moving. We had the collapse in 1929, and the hungry thirties. Then, President Roosevelt, that great President of the United States, came on the scene. Prices were down. Potatoes were 10 cents a barrel; copper was down to 9 cents a pound,
March 15, 1966	COMMONS
or something like that. Somebody told President Roosevelt that if he would raise the price of gold, he would raise prices. He raised the price of gold from $20.67 to $35 an ounce. This move did not raise world prices, but it certainly adjusted the exchanges around the world. At that time the pound in South Africa was $8; in Australia, $3 and in the West Indies it was something else. We could not possibly trade because the exchanges were all different. When President Roosevelt raised the price of gold to $35 an ounce, the exchanges of the world were adjusted to $35.
I know whereof I speak because at that time many factories were idle. Within a month when world trade became adjusted those factories were working and prices came up. Although I do not think it was the President's idea to bring up world prices, they were brought up owing to the restoration of world trade.
We have a different situation today. The United States is the banker of the world and the United States dollar is the world's unit of settlement, not the pound sterling. The pound sterling is backed by the U.S. dollar and if the U.S. dollar fails so does the pound sterling. The U.S. dollar is based on gold, according to the United States government.
In 1934 when gold was $35 an ounce the U.S. dollar was worth $1. Today the purchasing power of the U.S. dollar is only 44 cents. That is agreed to by all business magazines. Therefore how can 44 cents buy the same amount of gold that $1 bought in 1934? It is impossible.
The United States government owes $30 billion on demand. De Gaulle of France, or any of the central banks of Europe, can demand their money and the U.S. government must pay them in gold. The United States government is now proposing a new unit of settlement which is based on paper, known as the c.r.u. Countries put so much money into the monetary fund, and this new c.r.u. unit is based on paper, not on gold.
Why does the United States say that gold is worth $35 an ounce when the double eagle $20 gold piece of the United States is sold in Europe for $45. We sold $50 million Canadian gold to the United States for $50 million U.S.; but if we minted double eagles selling for $45 in Europe our gold would be worth twice what it is worth today.
I see no reason to continue participating in the International Monetary Fund. The fund is directed by the United States which, as far as I can see, uses it to further its own interests.
DEBATES	2749
Bretton Woods Agreements Act If that country does not wish to base its money on gold, it should do what we do in this country and base its money on the resources of the country, letting gold find its own value.
In 1934 many precious metals went up in value by 50 per cent, but gold remains the same. This is an impossible situation. Whether gold backs the currency or not, it must go up in price. Take, for example, the little Portuguese settlement of Macao off the coast of China. They imported $1,500 million in gold which can be bought in England a few cents per ounce over the $35 price. The Portuguese government takes a commission of $1 an ounce. That gold is hoarded. Every year the mines of the world produce $1,400 million in gold. Some $1 billion goes into hoarding and $400 million goes into our central banks.
We cannot go on in this way; yet the United States says it is not going to raise the price of gold. If you do not raise the price of gold you let the dollar go.
No bank in Canada will sell gold. Neither can it be bought in the United States. If you are found with a bar of gold in the United States you go to the penitentiary. You cannot buy gold in England as a citizen of that country, either. But we find citizens of the United States coming to Canada to buy up our gold mines. Little Longlac was bought up by United States citizens and they took the treasury and bought up other gold mines. You will find, Mr. Speaker, that citizens of the United States own most of the gold mines in Canada. This is because Canadians cannot mine their own gold, although United States citizens can own our gold mines. The United States should divorce its dollar from the gold standard and the dollar should become the international unit of payment.
We have the dollar in Canada. For a $50 bill we can get 50 $1 bills, or two $20 bills and a $10 bill, or we can get silver. But we cannot get gold. We can buy bar gold which is not minted, but we can sell it only at the bar gold price. What we should do internationally is divorce our money from the gold standard and let gold find its own value, in which event its price would go up.
For thousands of years gold has been the standard of credit on which everyone depends. The people of the world do not depend on paper but on gold. If the United States would divorce its dollar from the gold standard and would make the U.S. dollar the unit
March 15. 1966

Bretton Woods Agreements Act of settlement for the entire world, things would be all right. We would not have to contribute to the International Monetary Fund. The United States dollar would be the international unit of settlement, as was the pound sterling before the great world war.
There is no reason this cannot be done, but the United States government is as stubborn as a donkey and will not change its policy. They say the dollar is worth $1 in gold, but I say it is not; the purchasing power of the dollar is only 44 cents and is going down. Prosperity on the North American continent implies gradual inflation, which means that the dollar will go down in purchasing power.
I say that the establishment of the c.r.u. is a lot of baloney. When the price of gold changed in 1934 to $35 an ounce, it was said that the United States public had a "baloney" dollar. I say that when they imply that their dollar is worth $1 of gold they have a "baloney" dollar because their $1 is worth only 44 cents. Our gold is worth twice that, and more.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
I say we are acting like ostriches and burying our heads in the sand when we think we can distribute our gold around the world, letting speculators take advantage of this. We in Canada let our gold mines go down. Our gold production in Canada has gone down greatly, year after year. The result is that we take $15 million out of the taxpayers pockets to keep the gold mines going every year.
What has happened has not contributed to any new gold mines coming into being. What we want in this country is a policy that will develop new gold mines from coast to coast. We have such gold in our pre-Cambrian shield, but we are not doing anything about it. The United States is leading us in this respect. In this case, the policy of the United States is wrong, although I would say that it is right in a great many things. The United States is wrong in the conception of what gold is worth in the world. The whole of world opinion is against the United States in its conception about gold. Gold is the basis of all credit, and the sooner the authorities in the United States realize that, the better.
Contributions to the monetary fund and things like that to bolster our credit I do not think will be of benefit. The authorities in the United States ought to have common sense, because we look upon the United States dollar as the unit of settlement for the entire world, in the same way that we looked upon the pound sterling. We recognize that, but we 
say that gold ought to find its own level, and then the United States dollar in turn will find its level. That fundamentally is our feeling, because the United States dollar in purchasing power is now worth 44 cents, compared with 1934.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are a few comments I feel I must make on the Bretton Woods Agreements. It is really time to amend the legislation on the Bretton Woods agreements signed with the United States and various other countries.
Unfortunately, those agreements were approved in 1944 by the Liberals, who were then in office, and also by the Conservatives and the socialists, who were in the opposition. There is nothing surprising in that because when the International Monetary Fund was set up in 1944, under the Bretton Woods agreements, it was the old capitalist formula that prevailed. Three great capitalist countries had their formula adopted and it was that formula which prevailed and which the other countries had to accept. Three great countries hold among themselves a substantial part of the majority of the shares.
Instead of an institution controlled by just a few countries, quotas of equal value should be set for each country and equal voting rights provided for all members of the agreement.
The Bretton Woods agreements especially favour creditor nations like the United States without requiring them to balance their trade by accepting goods from other countries. That obligation is imposed on debtor nations.
When they established the gold standard, they gave creditor nations the right to wait and to insist upon being paid in gold or American dollars. There is the problem we have to solve. Until we do or as long as we do not take steps to reach better agreements with the United States and the other two greatest countries, we shall not be able to settle that problem.
That, Mr. Chairman, is the cause of the international balance of payments problem. The big countries take advantage of the small ones. Small countries are asked to pay their accounts in American currency or gold, which is practically impossible.
I fully agree with the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. McLean) who has just concluded his remarks, when he says that improvements can be found, that the Americans
March 15, 1966	COMMONS
dominate us and that our dollar is worth only 44 cents. He is perfectly right when he says that instead of converting our gold, we sell it to the United States at ridiculous prices. We fully agree on that.
It is very advantageous for the United States to come and develop our natural resources in Canada and mine our gold to take it home when we could convert that gold or exchange it, which would double its value for Canada.
The hon. member for Charlotte was perfectly right about that. We fully agree with him.
I ask those who will be called upon in committee to consider the Bretton Woods agreements to study the structure of the international monetary system and to find the solutions which Canada needs.
At this time, practically everyone agrees that we are exploited by the three larger countries which signed the Bretton Woods agreements and which, through their action, dominate all other nations. There is a lot of work to be done in that respect and I ask the government to appoint to the Commission experts in that field so that Canada will benefit to a greater extent from those agreements, will no longer be exploited by various nations, will be able one day to balance its international accounts and prosper like the other countries instead of devaluating its currency, giving discounts on its products to pay its international accounts, which is contrary to social justice.
There are other reforms to carry out in that field and I am convinced that the suggestions and good ideas of the hon. member for Charlotte will greatly help on the Liberal side. Frankly, something must be done in that respect.

Resolution reported and concurred in.

POWER-COLUMBIA RIVER-SAFETY OF HIGH ARROW DAM
speechtext:
It is
a thrilling experience, Mr. Speaker, to rise in this stimulating atmosphere, but what we lack in physical bodies we know we have here in spirit.
On March 14, I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs the following question:
In view of the fact, that the members of the standing committee on external affairs were assured that the High Arrow Dam was a completely safe structure would the minister inform the house why, in the report of the Columbia Treaty Permanent Engineering Board, which includes representatives of Canada and the United States, the board does not accept direct or implied responsibility, for the safety of the structures being built according to the Columbia River Treaty?
Now the Columbia River Treaty Permanent Engineering Board is composed of two representatives from Canada and two from the United States. The Canadian representatives are Mr. G. M. MacNabb, Chairman, a well known engineer, and Mr. A. F. Paget who is in charge of the water resources branch, British Columbia. The United States representatives are Mr. Wendell E. Johnson, Chairman, and Mr. Morgan D. Dubrow. This board is charged with the responsibility of making certain that the provisions of the Columbia River Treaty are carried out. I have in my hand the first annual report to the
March 15, 1968

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion governments of the United States and Canada of the Columbia River Treaty Permanent Engineering Board, dated December 31, 1965. Reading from this report I see that the duties and responsibilities of the board are outlined. However, I was surprised to read with respect to the activities of the board at page 11 the following paragraph:
The Board considered its responsibility for the safety of structures authorized for construction by the Treaty. The Board concluded that neither the duties specified in the Treaty nor its consideration of design data received from the Entities for the purpose of keeping fully informed regarding the projects gives the Board either a direct or implied responsibility for the safety of the structures or for the adequacy of their structural design. However, it was agreed that any apparent defects noted by the board would be promptly called to the attention of the Entities.
Now, Mr. Speaker, during the hearing of the Standing Committee on External Affairs when the Columbia River Treaty was under consideration, we were assured by Dr. Arthur Casagrande, a world wide authority on the building of dams and soil conditions, and also in respect of the damage that could be done by tremors and earthquakes, that the High Arrow dam, with which we were particularly concerned, was completely safe. Numerous people have written to me about this, because we must not forget that last year we had a tremor in southeastern British Columbia in which buildings were rocked in Trail, which is only 18 miles south of the High Arrow dam. We were assured that this dam was completely safe.
I was rather shocked to read in this report that the very board, whose responsibility we were assured it would be to see that the terms of the Columbia River Treaty were carried out, had failed to accept any responsibility for the safety of the structures being built under this treaty.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I regret having to keep the minister a few minutes after ten o'clock, because I know he would prefer to be in another place at this moment. Therefore I shall be as brief as possible. I do want him to explain to the house why the Columbia River Treaty Permanent Engineering Board made this decision after we were told that this board was responsible for seeing that the terms of the Columbia River Treaty were carried out. Part of those terms are to see that all the structures are safe.
Mr. Speaker, I shall look forward to the reply of the minister, because not only the member for Kootenay West, but also a good

many of the people whom I have the honour to represent, are interested. Before concluding I would suggest to the minister that this is a very interesting report. Would he take up the question of having copies made available for members of the house who wish to obtain them.

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister without Portfolio):
maintopic: POWER-COLUMBIA RIVER-SAFETY OF HIGH ARROW DAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that I appreciate that the hon. member for Kootenay West has brought up a very interesting point. I will make the answer as brief as I can and say that there is nothing within Article XV of the Columbia River Treaty which makes the permanent engineering board responsible specifically for the safety of construction sites. The responsibility for the safety of the dams lies under the aegis of the two contracting parties, namely the United States and Canada, as two separate entities.
I wish to say that the permanent engineering board, of course, is an international body which, if it had the responsibility for reviewing construction standards and, were it responsible for the safety of those dams, then what the hon. member really would be implying is that the engineers from the United States would have a veto over Canadian construction standards and construction methods.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Under the treaty the dams on the Canadian side of the border are the responsibility of the federal government, as delegated to the province of B.C., and the construction of the dams, the Libby dam in particular in the United States, is the responsibility of the United States government. I am very surprised, in view of the earlier representations of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), that he should imply that United States engineers should have a veto over Canadian construction standards.
I refer to page 4934 of Hansard for July 2, 1964 when he said, in a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin):
In view of the assurances given by him-
That is, the minister.
-to the committee . . . that the safety of the dams was known and satisfactory, would the minister inform the house whether he thinks it is necessary for the government of British Columbia to call in three United States engineers to clarify his assurances and to make sure he was giving the committee the facts?
March 15. 19G6	COMMONS
Of course, the answer was that Canadian engineers were perfectly capable of reviewing Canadian construction standards.
I want to say further that there is no suggestion in the Columbia treaty that either country may interfere with or dictate construction methods in the other country; yet this could be the case if the permanent engineering board were given the responsibility of passing judgment on the safety of the treaty structures.
As to the safety of the dams themselves, let me say that in Canada the British Columbia government has accepted federal responsibility for the construction of the Canadian dams, and the design of those dams is reviewed by five separate bodies. The first is the British Columbia Hydro and Power Authority, the second are the consultants to the Hydro Authority; the third is the British Columbia Water Rights Branch; the fourth is the consultants to the Water Rights Branch, and the fifth is a board of review consisting of five eminent United States and Canadian engineers.
I also recall that last year, on June 21, 1965, I replied to a question of the hon. member, as recorded at page 2672 of Hansard, when I talked about the safety factor. I said:
Every precaution in the interests of safety against possible damage from earthquakes, seepage, erosion, or other causes, has been taken in the design and in the construction requirements. This subject was considered in detail by the Standing Committee on External Affairs during its consideration of the Columbia river treaty and protocol, and in particular during its sessions on April 24 and April 28. 1964, when expert evidence on these aspects of the safety of the project was given-
1 went on to give the names of the people who had given that expert evidence. The hon. member and I had the privilege of serving on that committee together. We heard that evidence together. I am satisfied that not only has the safety of the dams been provided for, but I am also satisfied that proper control of that safety is effected by Canadian engineers, and that is the reason why the permanent engineering board, in its report, has given as its interpretation of the treaty that it does not bear the responsibility for supervision of safety construction standards.
